purpose: Explain architecture errors that Tab 1 should expose, including what they mean and what can happen if not corrected.
placement_reason: Stored under _project_reference/TAB_HELP so this is documentation/helper data only and does not change runtime behavior.
implementation_status_note: W022C/W022D help parity verified: all 25 Tab 1 architecture help categories are mapped to implemented Tab 1 architecture validation issue codes. This JSON is beginner-facing helper content and does not change runtime behavior.
display_lines: 1. Duplicate public symbols - Two or more files define or export the same public class, function, or constant name. A beginner can think of it like two workers wearing the same name tag.
2. Symbol shadowing - A local name hides another name with the same spelling. It is like putting a new label over an old label, so the original becomes hard to see.
3. Wrong owner box - Code lives in the wrong part of the system. It is like storing kitchen tools inside the bathroom cabinet.
4. Cross-box boundary violations - One part of the app reaches directly into another part that it should not control. It is like a cashier changing the chef's recipe without asking.
5. Circular imports - Two files depend on each other in a loop. File A needs File B, while File B needs File A.
6. Side effect on import - A module performs visible work just by being imported. Imports should define names, not start actions, change folders, write files, or launch tools.
7. Mixed responsibility files - One file tries to do too many unrelated jobs. It is like one person being the driver, mechanic, accountant, and doctor at the same time.
8. Stale or deprecated variants - Old versions, backup files, or temporary copies remain in the project and look active.
9. Misplaced tests - A test file exists, but it is in the wrong folder or tests the wrong target.
10. Test protection gap - Important active source code has no direct or indirect test protection, so future changes can break it without the validation workflow noticing.
11. Unsafe path and platform assumptions - The code assumes a path style, operating system, or encoding that may not match the real environment.
12. Canonical vs working-copy boundary errors - The app confuses the protected official JSON with the local AI working copy.
13. Generated artifact contract errors - Generated files do not match the expected format, name, location, or required sections.
14. Public API instability - A public function, class, or export changes without compatibility planning.
15. Dead code and unreachable files - Files or functions exist but nothing uses them.
16. Inconsistent source of truth - Two project documents or code sections disagree about what is active or correct.
17. Test asserts internal detail - A test depends on private implementation details instead of public behavior, making safe refactors look broken.
18. Import heaviness and slow startup risk - A lightweight tool imports heavy modules too early.
19. Bundle safety issues - A delivered ZIP changes too much, lacks a manifest, or modifies the wrong files.
20. Project-wide AI confusion risks - The project is arranged in a way that makes AI likely to choose the wrong file, owner, or symbol.
21. Cross-box public symbol collision - Different boxes expose the same public name. This is more specific than ordinary duplicates because it crosses architecture boundaries.
22. Shared mutable state coupling - Mutable state is shared across architecture boxes, so one box can silently change another box's runtime behavior.
23. Inconsistent error contract at boundaries - One box raises errors, another swallows errors, and another returns None. The boundary has no common rule.
24. Tests assert implementation internals instead of public contracts - A test checks private details instead of checking what the user or public API should observe.
25. Missing __all__ or uncontrolled public surface - A module does not clearly say which names are public. Everything can look exportable.
